title: The Body as a Memory Board
tagline: A medieval monk taught singers with the joints of one hand. You will use ten places on your body to keep ten things in order.
card: A monk's teaching hand, and your first fixed list of places: ten spots from head to toe that are always with you.
goal: you will learn ten fixed places on your body, use them to store ten items in order, and turn a hard name into something you can place.

left_off.q: What does the 'S' in SMASHIN' SCOPE stand for? (There are two ideas, one is 'senses'.)
left_off.a: S stands for Synaesthesia/senses, Sensuality and Symbolism: three of the twelve ways to make a picture richer.

left_off.q: What is substitution, and why do we use it?
left_off.a: Replacing a word you cannot picture with something you can see that sounds like it or stands for it. For example, Brazil becomes a giant bra.

left_off.q: Give three tools you could use to make a picture of a LAMP stronger.
left_off.a: For example: size (as big as a house), movement (it dances), colour (it is red), humour (it sings opera).

text: Northern Italy, about a thousand years ago. In the choir school of a cathedral, a monk named Guido, from the town of Arezzo, has a problem that every choirmaster had. The great church chants had no written notes that anyone could easily read. A boy learned each melody by listening to an older singer sing it again and again, and it could take many years to learn enough to sing in church.
Guido wanted a quicker way. He is remembered for several ideas, but the one that lasted longest was strangely simple. He taught his singers to use the palm of their own hand.

check.q: What was the problem Guido wanted to solve?
check.a: Singers had to learn each chant by ear, and it took many years to learn enough of them.

parts.talk: How do you learn a new song? How long does it take to be sure of it?

text: On the left hand, every fingertip and every joint stood for a note, from the lowest to the highest. The teacher pointed at the joints one after another while the boys sang, and the boys learned to think of a note and a place on the hand as the same thing. Later they could do it silently. The hand was a map of sound that they carried everywhere, and no one could lose it or forget it at home.

Even the names of the notes came from a song. Guido used a hymn to Saint John whose lines began with the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Each line began one note higher than the last, so the singers could hear what each name sounded like. Those syllables are the ancestors of do, re, mi.

check.q: How did the hand work as a memory device?
check.a: Each joint and fingertip stood for a note, so the learner could point to a place on the hand to recall a sound.

parts.talk: Why is your own body a good place to keep things? What are the advantages over a notebook?

text: The 'Guidonian hand' stayed in music books for centuries, drawn in the margins of manuscripts and printed textbooks. People simply found it useful. It was always with them, it was a fixed order, and it was easy to touch while they thought.

That is exactly what we want from our first memory place. In this lesson you will not use a hand but your whole body: ten places from head to toe, always in the same order. They are the simplest possible memory board.

check.q: Why does the body make a good memory board?
check.a: It is always with you, the order never changes, and you can touch or think about each place.

parts.talk: Which of your own body parts would you give the job of remembering your phone number? Why?

words.m: a fixed point you hang something on. A coat on a peg. Here: a fixed place in your memory.
one after the other in the right sequence. Say the days in order.
to fix one thing to another. Attach the picture to the nose.
to act on each other. The pizza interacts with your head.
a word that sounds like another word. "Bra" is a sound-alike for "Brazil".
easy to carry. Your body is a portable memory board.

source: The Guidonian hand is traditionally linked to Guido of Arezzo (about 991 to after 1033). Retold here in our own words.
method_heading: Ten pegs, always in the same order

method.x: A peg is a fixed place you hang a picture on. If the pegs never change and always come in the same order, they can hold a list for you.

method.cap: One to ten, head to toe. Use this order every single time.

items.x: Head, eyes, nose, mouth, neck, chest, stomach, legs, feet, toes. Do it until it is automatic. It takes a few minutes.

items.h: Turn each item into a picture.
items.x: If you cannot picture it, substitute a sound-alike (see lesson 2).

items.h: Put the picture ON the peg.
items.x: Make it touch, cover or attack that part of your body. You should feel it there.
It moves, it makes a noise, it has a smell.

items.h: To recall, walk down your body.
items.x: Start at the head, and see what is sitting on each place.

method.title: One item on one peg
lines: An old-fashioned telephone, as big as a watermelon, balanced on your head.
The cord is wrapped around your ears like a snake.
It keeps ringing, so your whole head vibrates.
method.pic: A watermelon-sized telephone ringing wildly on top of your head, its cord wrapped round your ears.

method.x: Turning a name into something you can place

Brazil is not a picture. But Brazil sounds like bra. So you place a giant red bra across your chest (peg 6), with straps made of snakes. Russia sounds like rushing: a torrent of water rushes down your head. Hard words always turn into something. If one resists, pick any sound-alike.

ten places.
one trip down the body.
same order
every time.
What the body can and cannot do

items: It is portable and instant. No building needed, and you can use it on a bus.
It holds ten. More would need places that are crowded or hard to tell apart. For longer lists you will use a building (lesson 4).
It can be reused once the list is no longer needed. Clear the pegs by imagining them empty and clean.

try.title: Item and peg: BANANA on EYES
try.prompt: Put a banana on peg 2, your eyes. Make it unforgettable. Use movement and at least one sense besides sight.
try.model: Two bright yellow bananas are strapped over your eyes like sunglasses, but they are dripping hot custard that runs down your cheeks. You can smell it, and every time you blink they squeak loudly.
checks: The banana is touching or acting on the eyes.
It moves or makes a sound.
I used a sense besides sight.

try.title: Item and peg: PIZZA on HEAD
try.prompt: Put a pizza on peg 1, your head, and an elephant on peg 4, your mouth. Write both pictures.
try.model: A huge pizza is melting over your head like a hat; the cheese runs down your neck. An elephant sits in your open mouth trumpeting, and it makes your whole jaw rumble.
checks: Each picture sits ON the peg.
Each moves or makes a sound.
The two pictures are very different from each other.

try.title: Hard names
try.prompt: Turn these into pictures you can place: Brazil on the chest (6), Canada on the nose (3), China on the mouth (4). Use a sound-alike for each. Write your three pictures.
try.model: Brazil = bra: a gigantic red bra strapped across your chest. Canada = can: a giant tin can crushed on your nose, its label peeling. China = china plates: crockery smashing in your open mouth, and you taste dust.
checks: I used a sound-alike for each.
Each picture sits on its peg.
None of my pictures is calm or still.

try.title: Which peg?
try.prompt: Match the item to the peg it should sit on.

try.q: Why is it important to use the pegs in the same order every time?
opts: So the order of the list is built into the pegs
Because the body only has one order
So the pictures can be smaller
try.why: The fixed order is the point. It gives the list its sequence automatically.

try.title: The walk
try.prompt: Say the ten pegs aloud in order while touching each place. Then say your three hard-word pictures (Brazil, Canada, China) as you touch chest, nose, mouth.

quiz.why: The picture must touch or act on the body part so you feel it there.

quiz.q: How many items can the body pegs usefully hold?
quiz.why: Ten. For more, use a palace (lesson 4).
1 head, 2 eyes, 3 nose, 4 mouth, 5 neck, 6 chest.

quiz.q: How do you recall a list stored on the body pegs?
opts: Walk down the body from the head, seeing each picture
Repeat the list as quickly as possible
quiz.why: The walk down the body brings the pictures back in order.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the first ten elements
challenge.intro: Put the first ten chemical elements on your ten body pegs, in order. Sound-alike hints: hydrogen = hydrant, helium = high voice or balloon, lithium = lit-up, beryllium = berry, boron = boring, carbon = car, nitrogen = night, oxygen = ox, fluorine = floor, neon = neon sign.
challenge.study: A picture for each, placed on pegs 1 to 10, head to toes. Then type them in order, one per line.

look_back.q: Name the three stages of memory.
Name three of the twelve SMASHIN' SCOPE tools.
look_back.a: For example: Movement, Humour, Colour, Exaggeration, Number, Symbolism.

look_back.q: How do you picture a word like justice?
look_back.a: Substitute: use something you can see that stands for it or sounds like it, such as a judge with scales.

look_back.q: When is forgetting fastest, and what should you do about it?
look_back.a: Right after learning, so review soon, then at longer gaps.

can_do: say the ten body pegs in order.
place a picture on a peg so I can feel it there.
turn a name I cannot picture into a sound-alike picture.
reflect: Where, in daily life, would a list of ten things be useful to hold for a day or two? (A shopping list, tasks, points for a talk.) How would you use the pegs?
